column4: After the rebuke for neglecting the orphan and not urging food for the miskin, this ayah describes inheritance being devoured without restraint; it shows wealth consumed in a way that withholds a dependent’s due.
The next ayah names intense love of wealth, locating the attachment behind the preceding neglect; it contrasts with the section’s food given despite the giver’s love for it.
The final ayah says they withhold ordinary aid; alongside pushing the orphan and not encouraging food, this makes practical refusal the opposite of the section’s mercy that reaches the hand.

Immediately before the statement that they did not urge feeding the poor, this ayah says they did not believe in God the Great; it reverses the section’s pairing of belief with mutual exhortation to mercy.
For a hunting violation during pilgrimage, the expiation may be food for miskin; it adds a specific duty to feed the needy from sacrificial provision beside the section’s hunger-day meal.

This ayah describes the servants of the Merciful as neither extravagant nor stingy in spending; against the section’s claim to have spent abundant wealth, it distinguishes measured provision from boasting about amount.
This ayah condemns those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s path; it gives a concrete opposite to directing wealth toward the hungry as the section requires.
The next ayah depicts that hoarded wealth as a punishment on the Day it is heated and used to mark them; it makes preserved wealth a failed answer to need.
Winds carry heavy clouds to dead land, rain brings forth fruit, and the scene ends by recalling resurrection; it gives a specific return of provision to the drought-struck land named in the section.
People rejoice when rain reaches them after having despaired before it; the ayah supplies the human turn from drought to relief behind the section’s famine-day urgency.
The next ayah asks the reader to see God’s mercy reviving earth after its death; it completes the rain scene as restoration of provision after scarcity.
Rain enters the earth as springs and brings out varied crops that later yellow and become debris; it makes the section’s drought and disappearing harvest a concrete cycle of provision.
Blessed rain brings out gardens and grain; this is a direct agricultural scene of the food whose absence makes the section’s famine day severe.
The next ayah calls the produce provision for servants and says dead land is revived by it; it completes the image of food returning to barren ground.
This command protects an orphan’s property until maturity and requires justice in measure and weight; it makes the section’s delayed or overlooked good a concrete duty of guardianship.
The covenant calls for good treatment of relatives, orphans, and needy people; it places the section’s specific feeding and orphan care within a direct command to treat these groups well.
The ayah rebukes withholding what is due to orphan girls and commands justice for orphans and weak children; it exposes a concrete form of the neglect the section counters.

Hypocrites ridicule believers who give generously and those who have only their effort to offer; this condemns contempt for contributions made under scarcity, beside the section’s care for the hungry.
Spending in God’s cause is likened to a grain that multiplies into abundant harvest; it contrasts wealth that seems spent with provision that bears fruit through giving.
The ayah says giving must not be followed by reminders or injury; it specifies how aid to the section’s vulnerable recipients can preserve their dignity.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm; it makes the section’s mercy a quality of treatment as well as food delivered.
This ayah warns that reminders, injury, and show can nullify charity; it marks the opposite of the section’s sincere, enacted compassion.
Those who spend seeking God’s approval are likened to a garden that yields abundantly with heavy rain and still yields with light rain; it pictures giving as fruitful even when provision is limited.
The command is to spend from good things earned and not choose inferior produce for giving; it sharpens what it means to feed the needy with real provision.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this names the fear of scarcity that can block the section’s call to feed during a hard day.
The continuation says spending is for the giver’s own good and should seek God’s face; it clarifies the section’s account of mercy as aid given without making the needy repay it.
In a family-maintenance context, a person of restricted provision is told to spend from what God has given; it supplies a concrete measure for giving when hardship limits the means.

The ayah names Quraysh’s recurring seasonal journeys; beside the section’s fed city and 106:4, it adds the city’s regular movement and provision setting to the claim that its people were fed from hunger.
